chapter: New Orleans, Havana and back to New York
title: Cuban rhythms and Mexican trumpet players
summary: He says Cuban flute and clarinet players and the rhythms were exciting, trumpeters weak, and jokes that Mexican trumpeters are good because of bullfights.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: So no music at all for four months. Did you listen to any music there? Was there any interesting music being played in Havana?

interesting. But outside of a couple of flute players, the horn players weren't -- the greatest brass players, I mean trumpet players, are Mexican. And in Cuba the trumpet players were terrible. Whereas, they had tremendous guys that played flute and the clarinet. There were saxophone players there, but they'd more or less concentrate on the flute, because they weren't big bands then. They were smaller bands. But the rhythms were very exciting.
Is there any particular reason you know of why the good trumpet players are Mexican and not Cuban?
They don't have bull fights in Cuba.
You know, they have to have some pretty good trumpet players for the bull fights.
Yes. That's what Cat Anderson told me. His biggest inspiration was Rafael Mendez.
So did you carry any Cuban rhythms back to your music in the United States?
Well, sure, I played maracas a little bit later, in Barney Bigard's Orchestra.
Of course, of course. Direct from Havana.
